parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Put the decision on page one
parts.body:
An executive memo should let a busy reader decide even if the meeting is cut short. Its first paragraph gives the requested action, accountable decision maker, amount and scope, deadline, and consequence of delay. State the business problem with a baseline. Then explain why this decision belongs with this executive under the company's delegated authority.

Use a compact sequence: request; evidence and context; credible options; recommendation and economics; material risks; assumptions; decision rule and next checkpoint. A one-page cover and an appendix often work better than squeezing evaluation results into tiny type. The reader should be able to disagree with your assumptions without guessing what they are.

Separate facts, forecasts, and judgment. For example, six weeks of observed handle time may be a fact; next year's volume is a forecast; a recommendation to buy instead of build is judgment. Attach the measurement method, source, and date for the few figures carrying the recommendation. A confident number without a denominator can mislead more than a range that exposes uncertainty.

example.title: An opening request
example.body: Approve a CAD 350,000 capped pilot of a claims drafting assistant for 12 weeks, limited to internal adjusters. The claims VP owns the decision; privacy and security must clear data access before testing. Return for expansion approval only if reviewed draft accuracy and cost per completed case meet the agreed thresholds. Figures are illustrative.

exercise.title: Write the first paragraph
exercise.body: Pick one use case. In 90 words, name the action, owner, cap, scope, deadline, baseline, and next gate. Have a peer identify the exact decision without reading any appendix.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: governance and documentation

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Compare options on the same basis
parts.body:
Compare buying an enterprise tool, building on an API, and deferring the investment. Use the same time horizon, eligible users, data assumptions, and outcome measure for every option. Include integration, licensing or usage, evaluation, security, support, training, and exit costs. A cheap model call may sit inside an expensive operating workflow. Deferral has a cost or benefit too: it can preserve cash while a dependency is fixed, or leave a measurable service problem untouched.

Use ranges when utilization or labor savings are uncertain. A simple scenario table can show low, base, and high adoption, but name the assumptions driving each scenario. Identify reversible choices, such as a narrow pilot with a contractual exit, and harder commitments, such as a multiyear vendor lock-in or a new team. Do not average a serious privacy concern into a numeric score with cosmetic features. Make any non-negotiable constraint visible before the weighted comparison.

A decision table should end in a recommendation with a reason. If the same option wins under every scenario because the scores were chosen to fit the answer, ask someone else to challenge the weights.

example.title: One basis for three options
example.body: Illustrative decision memo: internal claims drafting, 20,000 eligible cases a year, current 18-minute draft time and 10% correction rate, same target for every route: save four minutes per reviewed case without raising corrections. At 50% adoption and CAD 40 per hour of usable capacity, gross modeled capacity value is CAD 26,667 a year, before review and run cost; it is not cash savings. Buy costs CAD 520,000–680,000 over 12 months and launches in four months; API build costs CAD 470,000–790,000 and launches in six; defer costs CAD 80,000 in data cleanup while the current workflow continues. Both launch options fail if claim-text rights or vendor terms prohibit the proposed use. Figures are invented; these economics would reject either full rollout on productivity alone.

exercise.title: Build a decision table
exercise.body: Compare buy, build, and defer over 12 months. Include benefit, full cost range, launch time, data exposure, integration dependency, exit cost, and a condition that disqualifies an option. Ask the CFO to challenge one assumption.

sources: OPC Canada: assessing third-party service providers

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Make the risk and uncertainty actionable
parts.body:
A risk line needs an event, consequence, owner, proposed treatment, and evidence gate. 'Privacy risk: medium' does not tell an executive whether the vendor may train on customer data or whether the company can delete it. Name the contract term, data flow, review owner, and decision that depends on it. For EU operations, record whether counsel has classified the proposed use and checked applicable AI Act and data protection obligations. For Canadian personal information, identify the governing privacy regime and intended purpose.

Use a sensitivity test to reveal which assumption changes the recommendation. If adoption falls from 60% to 20%, what happens to cost per successful case? If an evaluation finds an unacceptable error rate, can the pilot be narrowed to draft assistance with mandatory review? Set a stop condition before the team becomes attached to the implementation.

The memo should identify who may accept residual risk. A CAIO can explain a risk and recommend a treatment, but cannot silently waive a security or privacy control belonging to another authority. Document required consultation, any unresolved disagreement, escalation path, and expiry date for an exception.

example.title: A risk and sensitivity gate
example.body: At 20% adoption, the modeled annual capacity value in the preceding example falls to CAD 10,667, while the quoted fixed costs remain. Recommend only a CAD 60,000 capped discovery phase to validate data rights, baseline, adoption intent, and an additional revenue or quality benefit. The claims VP decides on that spend; privacy and security owners must clear data use before any real records enter a vendor system. The VP returns in six weeks with a buy, build, or defer recommendation. If the vendor cannot meet the data requirement, use approved de-identified tests or reject that option. Figures are illustrative.

exercise.title: Stress-test the recommendation
exercise.body: Choose the two assumptions with the largest effect on your recommendation. Vary each, state when a different option wins, and identify the evidence owner and date. Write one release stop condition.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Close the loop after the decision
parts.body:
A memo is useful after approval only if its conditions can be checked. Record the decision, scope, funding cap, accountable owner, reviewers, assumptions accepted, stop conditions, and next checkpoint. Translate the requested evidence into a short evaluation plan: sampling method, business baseline, error severity, full cost, and affected user groups. Put the plan where operations can find it.

At the checkpoint, compare actual results with the memo's forecasts. Explain divergences before asking for more money. If volume was half the forecast, show the effect on unit economics. If a quality threshold failed, report affected cases and the corrective action. An extension is a new decision with a cost and end date, rather than an automatic reward for activity.

Keep earlier versions and decision records. They reveal how judgment improved, which assumptions proved weak, and whether the company respected its own gates. A later board update can cite the decision history instead of reconstructing it from memory.

example.title: A checkpoint that changes course
example.body: The pilot met its draft-time target but missed the reviewed error threshold. Management approves four weeks of targeted correction within the existing cap, holds customer-facing expansion, and asks for a fresh blind sample. No new funding is committed until the retest.

exercise.title: Write the follow-up note
exercise.body: Assume your preferred option delivered 70% of forecast adoption and had twice the expected correction rate. In 150 words, recommend continue, narrow, pause, or stop. Cite the original gate, actual evidence, owner, and next date.
